llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper identifies a critical flaw in current Online Continual Learning (OCL) evaluations: they disregard training time and computational constraints, which is unrealistic for real-world high-throughput data streams. The main contribution is the proposal of a practical real-time evaluation protocol for OCL that explicitly factors in training computational complexity, where the data stream does not pause for model training. Key findings include demonstrating that a simple Experience Replay (ER) baseline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art OCL methods under this new real-time evaluation. The research suggests that most existing OCL literature is tailored to impractical stream types and that a paradigm shift is needed to consider computational cost in the development of online continual learning methods.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The core methodology introduces a 'stream-model relative complexity' (CS) metric. CS(A)=1 means an OCL method A can update its model before the next data reveals, while CS(A)=k>1 signifies the stream is k-times faster, resulting in delayed model updates and skipped training batches. The evaluation protocol involves continuous predictions by the current model version as new data arrives, with model training and updates occurring only when computational budget allows, based on CS. Computational complexity (FLOPs) is used to determine CS, normalized against a simple ER baseline. For fair comparison, particularly in 'slow stream' scenarios, a modified baseline (ER++) is proposed, which performs additional gradient steps to computationally match more complex OCL methods, ensuring all methods operate with an equivalent computational budget without skipping stream steps.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted under 'fast stream' and 'slow stream' scenarios. The primary dataset used is CLOC, a large-scale online continual learning dataset with 39 million time-stamped images and 712 geolocation labels, exhibiting natural distribution shifts. Dataset splits included 5% for hyperparameter selection, 1% held-out for backward/forward transfer (reported in appendix), and the remainder for training and online evaluation. Benchmarked OCL methods included regularization-based (RWalk, ACE, LwF), learning rate scheduler (PoLRS), and sampling-based (GSS, MIR) approaches, against the ER baseline and its modified versions (ER--, ER++). The main evaluation metric was Average Online Accuracy, measuring adaptation to incoming stream samples. Supplementary experiments included small-scale datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100), pre-training-free scenarios, and variations in stream speed and gradient descent steps. The backbone was ImageNet pre-trained ResNet50 (or reduced ResNet18 for small-scale), trained with SGD, a batch size of 256 (128 stream + 128 memory), and a default replay buffer size of 4x10^4 samples.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The observed Average Online Accuracy for ER and ER++ (around 20-35%) indicates significant room for improvement in OCL methods. The ER baseline's strong performance might be partially attributed to potential temporal correlations within the CLOC dataset. While ER showed superior online adaptation, its information retention (backward transfer) was slightly worse than some other methods. Furthermore, the paper highlights that traditional backward transfer metrics might be less relevant for real-time OCL with natural distribution shifts, where current stream samples are most important. Similarly, forward transfer, as a running average, may be misleading, as near-future distributions are often more critical than far-future ones, suggesting a need for metrics focused on immediate adaptation.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future work could focus on designing new OCL datasets with reduced temporal dependencies to avoid potential biases towards methods like Experience Replay. Another direction involves developing OCL methods that can simultaneously optimize both online adaptation (achieving high Average Online Accuracy) and information retention (improving backward transfer). The paper also implicitly suggests a broader future research direction to foster a paradigm shift in the CL community, encouraging the development of methods that prioritize computational efficiency and real-time deployment considerations from the outset, rather than relying on expensive optimization routines.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Current CL research shows that task ordering strongly influences forgetting and forward transfer, yet there is no scalable, data-driven scheduler that (1) works with billion-parameter backbones, (2) jointly optimises for low gradient interference and high task similarity, and (3) respects wall-clock and memory budgets of real-time continual evaluation. Most work either assumes a fixed stream, relies on costly exhaustive search, or uses heuristic similarity measures that ignore stability-plasticity dynamics. The key challenge is to design an on-the-fly curriculum policy that selects the next task (or mini-batch) so as to minimise worst-case forgetting while maximising positive transfer, without introducing prohibitive compute overhead.
Methods: We propose GOST-CL (Gradient-Optimal-Similarity Task Curriculum for Continual Learning).
1. Dual Signal Estimation  – For every incoming task T_k we compute:
   a) Similarity score S_kj with each past task j via a fast low-rank Optimal Transport Dataset Distance (OTDD-Lite) computed in the frozen backbone representation.
   b) Interference score I_kj = E_b[ ∇θ L_k · ∇θ L_j ] estimated with one LoRA gradient probe (8-bit) using a mini-batch b.  Both are O(d·r) where r≪d.
2. Task Utility  – Define U_k = Σ_j  w_s S_kj  –  w_i |I_kj| where weights are tuned on a held-out stream slice.
3. Meta-Scheduler  – Formulate task selection as a bandit problem. At each step the scheduler observes U_k for the next M unseen tasks in a look-ahead buffer and picks the argmax under a fixed compute budget. It learns an uncertainty-aware policy via Thompson sampling so ordering improves over time.
4. Efficient Adaptation  – The learner is a 1-3B parameter ViT-G/14 backbone kept frozen + InfLoRA adapters (rank-64, nf4) per task. Only the adapter of the currently selected task is updated; past adapters stay frozen (no forgetting by design) but can be merged when similarity >τ to save memory.
5. Stability-Aware Loss  – Add Dynamic Gradient Calibration (DGC) term on the shared LayerNorms to further suppress interference.
6. Complexity Guard  – All scheduling computations are capped at <5% of one training iteration FLOPs, satisfying real-time continual evaluation (CS≤1).
Experimental Setup: Datasets: Split-ImageNet-R (10 tasks, 50 classes each), Split-CIFAR-100 (20 tasks), and CTrL-Sin/Sout 50-task streams. Each stream is reshuffled into 3 variants: Random, Semantic (WordNet), and Hard (max dissimilarity) to test robustness.
Models: ViT-H/14 (630 M) and ViT-G/14 (1.8 B) pre-trained on ImageNet-21K; adapters as above.
Baselines: Random order, OTDD-only ordering, Gradient-only ordering, Fixed curricula (easy→hard), and Oracle (post-hoc optimal). Learners: Finetune-Full, LoRA, InfLoRA, and ER-Memory (uniform sampling) to isolate ordering benefit.
Metrics: ACC, BWT, FWT, min-ACC, WC-ACC, WF10, compute-overhead %, peak GPU-mem, time-to-threshold. Evaluation uses ContinualEvaluationPhasePlugin (ρ_eval=1) with real-time constraint.
Ablations: remove interference term, vary look-ahead M, vary adapter rank, swap OTDD-Lite with cosine similarity.
Reproducibility: code + configs + Docker, seeds×3, wandb logs.
Result: We expect GOST-CL to:
• improve average ACC by +4-6 pp and min-ACC by +8-10 pp over Random order across all streams.
• halve BWT (e.g., −0.12→−0.06) and raise FWT by ~0.03.
• match Oracle within 80 % on ACC while using <5 % extra FLOPs (compute guard satisfied).
• out-perform OTDD-only and Gradient-only heuristics by ~3 pp ACC, showing benefit of joint signal and bandit learning.
• retain real-time CS≈1 (no skipped batches) and memory growth <15 % versus baseline InfLoRA.
Conclusion: GOST-CL demonstrates that intelligent task ordering can be made practical for billion-parameter backbones under real-time constraints. By combining fast OT dataset distances with lightweight gradient-interference probes and a bandit scheduler, it closes most of the stability gap without expensive replay or full fine-tuning. The method is backbone-agnostic, memory-aware, and orthogonal to adapter choices, paving the way for curriculum-aware deployment of foundation models in continual settings. Future work can extend the scheduler to mini-batch granularity, unsupervised task discovery, and reinforcement-learning domains, further enhancing lifelong autonomy of large models.
